title: Latency regression signals for rollouts (runtime input)
content:
Context
- This is runtime team guidance for the auto-rollback-on-SLO-breach project: what latency signals are meaningful for LLM inference rollouts, how tail behaves when batching/scheduling changes, and which windows are most reliable for automated decisions.
- Assumption: rollouts are scoped by {route/service, model + version, region, customer tier} and can be canary or A/B.

TL;DR recommendations (what we’d trust for auto-actions)
1) Track and evaluate separately:
   - TTFT (time-to-first-token) p95 and p99
   - TPOT (time-per-output-token) p95 and p99 (a.k.a. decode throughput in latency form)
   - End-to-end request latency p95 and p99 (still useful, but can hide what broke)
   - Error rate (5xx + upstream timeouts) as a separate fast-burn signal
2) The highest-signal “tail” metric for customer experience tends to be TTFT p99 during load/queueing regressions and TPOT p99 during kernel/quantization/runtime regressions.
3) For automation, prefer a dual-window burn-rate style evaluation (fast + slow) with minimum sample gating and a rollout-step holdoff to avoid flapping.

Which percentiles matter (and why)
- p50: good for diagnosing average throughput changes but too forgiving for auto-rollback. We keep it for dashboards, not as a trigger.
- p95: often catches regressions early with less noise than p99; good as a “slow-burn confirmation” window.
- p99: closest to “users feel it” and most sensitive to queueing and head-of-line blocking. Noisier; must be gated with sample size and debounced.

Recommended latency metrics to use as rollback signals
A) TTFT (time-to-first-token)
- Definition: from request accepted by Redwood API/gateway to first token emitted on stream.
- Why it’s high-signal: TTFT spikes quickly when queues grow, batching policy changes, admission control changes, or prefix cache behavior changes.
- Use cases:
  - Canary rollout causing scheduler inefficiency → TTFT p99 up, even if decode is stable.
  - Over-aggressive batching → TTFT up (more time waiting for batch fill), sometimes with better TPOT.

B) TPOT (time-per-output-token) / decode latency
- Definition: (end_to_end_latency - ttft) / output_tokens. (Use a robust metric implementation; exclude trivially short outputs where division explodes.)
- Why it’s high-signal: detects regressions in decode kernels, quantization profile changes, KV cache path changes, or GPU contention.
- Use cases:
  - New model build/version has worse decode efficiency → TPOT p95/p99 worsens, TTFT may stay flat.

C) End-to-end request latency
- Still valuable, but is a composite of (queue wait + prefill + decode + network).
- Use e2e p95/p99 as a backstop and for customer-facing reporting, but for auto-actions we generally prefer TTFT + TPOT because they point to the failure mode.

D) Queue wait / scheduler delay (if available in monitor provider)
- If we can export “time waiting before first compute” (queue_wait_ms), it’s one of the best leading indicators for saturation.
- Queue wait p99 can be a fast-burn signal, but it is also the most sensitive to traffic shifts (baseline/canary split changes) so apply conservative debounce.

Breakdown dimensions that are actually useful (and worth the cardinality)
Core dimensions (should exist on all rollout SLO queries)
- route (or service + endpoint)
- model
- model_version (or build id)
- region
- customer_tier (hosted/self-serve vs dedicated vs private; and/or enterprise tier)
- rollout_id / experiment_id (needed to correlate to a specific rollout step)

Strongly recommended (use buckets to control cardinality)
- prompt_tokens_bucket (e.g., 0–128 / 129–512 / 513–2k / 2k+)
- max_tokens_bucket (requested max output)
- output_tokens_bucket (actual output)
- cache_hit (prefix/KV cache hit yes/no; or hit_rate_bucket)

Nice-to-have for diagnosis (not required for auto-rollback triggers)
- gpu_sku (A10/L4/A100/H100/etc.)
- runtime_profile (quantization profile, attention kernel, paged-KV on/off)
- batch_size_bucket (1 / 2–4 / 5–8 / 9–16 / 16+)

Dimensions we should avoid in SLO-trigger evaluation (too high cardinality / too unstable)
- tenant_id / customer_id (use customer_tier; tenant-level can be for deep dives only)
- exact prompt length, exact output length (always bucket)
- request_id correlation as a label (logs/traces are fine; metrics labels are not)

How tail latency behaves under batching / scheduling changes
This is the core runtime nuance: batching can improve throughput and even p50 while harming p99 in specific regimes.

1) Continuous batching and head-of-line blocking
- When we allow large/long sequences into the same decode batch, long sequences can dominate GPU time slices.
- Impact pattern:
  - TPOT p50 may improve (better GPU utilization)
  - TPOT p99 can degrade (a few very long decodes cause stragglers)
  - e2e p99 may degrade even if average is stable
- Mitigation (runtime-side): batch composition constraints (length-aware batching), max time-in-batch, or separate queues by length bucket.
- Monitoring implication: always bucket by prompt/output length when investigating tail spikes; otherwise we’ll attribute incorrectly to “model regression.”

2) Batch fill delay and TTFT
- Aggressive batching targets (waiting to fill batches) add queueing delay before first token.
- Impact pattern:
  - TTFT p99 increases; TTFT p95 sometimes increases too
  - TPOT may improve (larger batch => better GPU efficiency)
- Rollout implication: when experimenting with batching parameters, TTFT is the canary signal. If we auto-rollback on e2e only, we may rollback unnecessarily without knowing it’s an expected tradeoff.

3) Cache warming and false positives in first minutes of a rollout step
- Prefix/KV cache hit rates often reset or shift when a model version changes, or when traffic splits change.
- Early in rollout, canary traffic can be “colder” than baseline (fewer repeated prefixes, less stable batch composition).
- Impact pattern:
  - TTFT and prefill time look worse for canary for ~2–10 minutes, then converge
- Recommendation: add a holdoff after each step transition (see windows below) and require minimum samples.

4) Saturation vs kernel regressions: distinguishing signatures
- Saturation/queueing regressions:
  - TTFT p99 spikes sharply
  - queue_wait_ms increases
  - GPU utilization high + queue depth increasing
  - error rate may increase via timeouts
- Kernel/model regressions (decode efficiency):
  - TPOT p95/p99 worsens
  - TTFT may be flat
  - GPU utilization may be similar, but tokens/sec drops

Recommended alert/evaluation windows for automated rollback
These are tuned to be actionable but robust to metric lag + rollout step transitions.

A) Dual window approach (fast + slow)
- Fast burn: 5m window
  - Primary purpose: catch acute regressions quickly (timeouts, sudden tail blowups)
  - Risk: noisy at low volume; must have minimum sample gating
- Slow burn: 30m window
  - Primary purpose: confirm sustained regression and avoid flapping on short spikes

B) Minimum sample gating (don’t trust tails with tiny N)
- For p99 evaluation, we need enough volume per scope. Suggested gates (pick one approach and be consistent):
  - Requests-based: min 300 requests in the evaluation window for p99; min 100 for p95
  - Token-based: min 50k output tokens in window for TPOT p99; min 20k for TPOT p95
- If below min samples: treat as “insufficient data” and do not auto-rollback; optionally auto-pause with a clear audit reason if policy says “fail-closed.”

C) Step transition holdoff / debounce
- Holdoff after changing traffic split or advancing rollout step: 3–5 minutes recommended.
  - Rationale: cache warming + batch composition stabilization + telemetry aggregation lag
- Debounce for decisions: require 2 consecutive fast-window breaches OR 1 fast-window + 1 slow-window breach (preferred).
- Cooldown after an auto-action: 15–30 minutes before evaluating again for further actions on the same rollout id, to prevent oscillation.

D) Metric staleness considerations
- If monitor timestamps are stale (e.g., last point older than 2x scrape interval or >3 minutes), do not trigger rollback.
- For staleness, we prefer “pause rollout” over “rollback” (rollback could be wrong if we’re blind).

Suggested default triggers (qualitative, not final policy numbers)
- TTFT p99 regression triggers are generally the best early-warning for saturation.
- TPOT p99 regression triggers are best for runtime/model regressions.
- If we must have a single latency trigger, use e2e p99, but we should still record TTFT/TPOT in the audit snapshot so humans can diagnose quickly.

Operational notes / common gotchas
- Tail metrics will move when:
  - traffic mix changes (prompt lengths, output lengths)
  - traffic splits change (canary at 5% has different cache + batching behavior)
  - request caps change (max_tokens default changed)
- Therefore, any automated decision should capture (in the audit event): the length buckets, cache hit rate, and traffic volume at time of decision.

Instrumentation / dashboarding asks to Observability (so runtime can debug quickly)
- For any auto-action event detail panel, show at minimum (for the rollout scope):
  - TTFT p95/p99 trend (baseline vs canary)
  - TPOT p95/p99 trend (baseline vs canary)
  - e2e p95/p99 trend
  - request rate, output token rate
  - cache hit rate trend
  - queue wait or queue depth if available
- If there’s only room for one chart: TTFT p99 + request rate.

Open questions / follow-ups
- Do we have a first-class TTFT metric in the SLO toolkit for all routes (hosted + dedicated + private), or is it only in tracing today?
- Can the monitor provider return both percentile values and sample counts per window per scope reliably? We need sample counts for gating.
- For A/B tests where both variants serve meaningful traffic, do we evaluate absolute SLO breach for the “new” variant, or relative regression vs baseline, or both?

Notes to self (runtime)
- When someone says “p99 got worse,” first ask: TTFT or TPOT? If TTFT -> look at queue/batching/admission control; if TPOT -> look at kernels/model build/quant profile.
- If we later add saturation signals into auto-actions, queue_wait_ms + timeout rate will outperform GPU utilization (util is frequently high even when healthy).
